facts.text: On this date in 1851, the New York Times published its first edition — then called the New-York Daily Times — selling for one cent. It cost a penny for 75 years before inflation ended the tradition.

On this date in 1931, Japan staged the Mukden Incident, blowing up its own railway in Manchuria and blaming China. The fabricated attack launched a 14-year occupation and set the template for 20th-century false-flag warfare.

Mongolia has a population density of 2 people per square kilometer — making it the least densely populated sovereign nation on Earth, yet it sustains a capital city, Ulaanbaatar, that holds 45% of all Mongolians.
More people live inside a 40-kilometer radius of Tokyo than in all of Canada. The greater Tokyo metro area, at roughly 37 million people, is the largest human settlement ever to exist on Earth.

The entire country of Liechtenstein has no airports. Its 39,000 residents travel through Switzerland or Austria for every flight, yet Liechtenstein maintains one of the highest GDPs per capita on the planet.
On this date in 1873, Jay Cooke & Company collapsed, triggering a panic that shuttered the NYSE for ten days — the longest closure in its history until 9/11.
On September 18, 1850, the US passed the Fugitive Slave Act. Cotton futures in New York rose the following week as Southern plantation output was seen as secured.
The S&P 500 has never closed at an exact round number. The index has passed through 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, and 5000 — but never ended a session precisely there.
Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway once held so much cash that its Treasury bill portfolio made it one of the largest single creditors of the US government.
The Dutch East India Company, at its 1637 peak, had a market cap equivalent to roughly $8 trillion in today's dollars — larger than Apple, Microsoft, and Nvidia combined.
On this date in 1970, Jimi Hendrix died — and the iron in his blood was forged inside a dying star. Every atom of iron in every human body was born in a supernova.
Your skeleton is not static. Every decade, you replace nearly all of it, one osteoclast and osteoblast at a time. The bones you were born with are long gone.
On September 18, 1977, Voyager 1 took the first photograph of Earth and Moon together in a single frame — from 7.25 million miles away, both fit inside a thumbnail.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A teaspoon of its material would weigh roughly a billion tons on Earth.
Trees in a forest share carbon and distress signals through fungal networks connecting their roots. A Douglas fir under attack can warn its neighbors within hours.
On this day in 1793, George Washington laid the Capitol's cornerstone. It was lost almost immediately and has never been found.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid — by about 500 years.
On this day in 1947, the CIA was born. It is younger than the NFL.
Oxford University began teaching students before the Aztec Empire existed. It predates Tenochtitlán by roughly 200 years.
The fax machine was invented in 1843 — before the American Civil War, before the telephone, and 44 years before the Eiffel Tower.
Sonder (n.): the realization that each passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Coined by John Koenig in The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, 2012 — now used as if it always existed.
Hiraeth (n.): a Welsh longing for a home you cannot return to, or perhaps never had. Untranslatable because no other language presumed to name an ache this precise.
On this day in 1709, Samuel Johnson was born — the man who spent nine years writing a dictionary defining 42,773 words, including 'lexicographer: a harmless drudge.'
Petrichor (n.): the smell of rain on dry earth. Named in 1964 by Australian scientists Bear and Thomas, who blended the Greek for stone and the fluid in the veins of gods.
Vellichor (n.): the strange wistfulness of used bookshops. Another Koenig coinage — proof that a word only needs one careful author to feel ancient.

On this date in 2017, China's central bank declared ICOs illegal and ordered all completed token sales to refund investors — triggering a 40% Bitcoin crash within days that fully recovered in under six weeks.
On this date in 2021, El Salvador's Bitcoin Law took effect, making BTC the world's first cryptocurrency granted legal tender status, requiring all businesses capable of processing it to accept it.

The Bitcoin genesis block contains the embedded text 'The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks' — Satoshi's timestamp doubles as a permanent editorial comment on the system being replaced.

Ethereum's EIP-1559, activated in August 2021, introduced a base fee that is burned rather than paid to miners — by 2023, over 3.5 million ETH had been destroyed, making the asset periodically deflationary.

The most expensive single NFT sale by on-chain transaction cost was Beeple's 'Everydays' at $69.3M — the buyer, Metakovan, paid in WETH settled on Ethereum, meaning the entire transfer is auditable to the block.

On this date in 2017, Demis Hassabis presented AlphaGo Zero at a Nature press briefing — a system that learned Go from scratch with zero human game data and surpassed all prior versions within 40 days.
On this date in 2020, OpenAI released the GPT-3 API to its first outside developers, beginning the quiet commercialization of large language models before most of the industry had noticed.
The training run for GPT-4 is estimated to have consumed roughly 50 gigawatt-hours of electricity — comparable to the annual consumption of 4,500 average US households, for a single model checkpoint.

Transformers were proposed in 2017 by eight Google researchers. Within five years, the architecture had displaced nearly every competing approach across vision, audio, protein folding, and code generation simultaneously.
Claude Shannon's 1950 paper 'Programming a Computer for Playing Chess' described learned evaluation functions and tree pruning — concepts that took 65 years to fully realize in AlphaZero.
